source_refs.note: Practice short questions written from Chapter 5 (PDF 126-152, printed 123-149); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 5 (Data Analytics), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is model building?
blocks.explanation: Model building is the process of creating simplified representations of complex problems. It helps in understanding, analysing and solving real-world issues by focusing on key elements.

book_ref.quote: Model building is the process of creating simplified representations of complex problems

blocks.prompt: 2 Define a model and state what it helps us to do.
blocks.explanation: A model is a simplified way of looking at a complex problem or situation. It helps to understand, explain or predict how things work.

book_ref.quote: It helps to understand, explain, or predict how things work

blocks.prompt: 3 Why is a model compared with a map of a city?
blocks.explanation: A map helps us navigate a city by showing only roads and landmarks. In the same way, a model helps us understand a problem by focusing on the most important parts and leaving out unnecessary details.

book_ref.quote: a model helps us understand a problem by focusing on the most important parts and leaving out unnecessary details

blocks.prompt: 4 How is a student's study plan an example of a model?
blocks.explanation: To decide how much time to spend on each subject, the student makes a study plan. It simplifies the schedule by focusing on the important subjects and ignoring less relevant tasks, so it is a model.

book_ref.quote: To decide how much time to spend on each subject, the student creates a study plan

blocks.prompt: 5 Give two reasons why models are useful in decision making.
blocks.explanation:
1. Models give a structured way to think about a problem and make complicated information easier to work with.
2. They help us consider different outcomes before making a choice.

book_ref.quote: They take complicated information and make it easier to work with

blocks.prompt: 6 How does a model help a farmer?
blocks.explanation: By studying weather patterns and soil conditions, the model helps the farmer predict the right time to plant crops, which increases the chances of a good harvest.

book_ref.quote: which increases the chances of a good harvest

blocks.prompt: 7 Name three fields in which models are commonly applied.
blocks.explanation:
1. Weather forecasting
2. Financial predictions
3. Scientific research

book_ref.quote: Some common fields where models are applied include weather forecasting, financial predictions, and scientific research

blocks.prompt: 8 How are models used in weather forecasting?
blocks.explanation: Meteorologists collect data such as temperature, humidity and wind speed, and then use models to analyse this data and forecast future weather conditions.

book_ref.quote: and then use models to analyze this data and forecast the weather

blocks.prompt: 9 What do banks and companies predict with models?
blocks.explanation: Banks and companies use models to predict economic trends, stock prices and even customer behaviour.

book_ref.quote: Models are also very important in the financial world

blocks.prompt: 10 What is statistics? Name its basic concepts.
blocks.explanation: Statistics is a branch of mathematics that helps us understand and analyse data and summarize large sets of information simply. Basic concepts: descriptive statistics, measures of central tendency, measures of dispersion and probability.

book_ref.quote: By using statistics, we can summarize large sets of information in a simple way

blocks.text: 5.2.1 Measures of Central Tendency (Mean, Median, Mode)

blocks.prompt: 11 What are measures of central tendency? Name them.
blocks.explanation: Measures of central tendency help us find the centre or typical value in a set of data. The three main measures are mean, median and mode.

book_ref.quote: Measures of central tendency help us find the

blocks.prompt: 12 Find the mean of the marks 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24.
blocks.explanation: Mean = sum of values / number of values = (12 + 15 + 18 + 21 + 24)/5 = 90/5 = 18.

book_ref.quote: The mean is the average of all the numbers in a data set

blocks.prompt: 13 Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 3, 5, 11, 3 and 8.
blocks.explanation: Arranged in order: 3, 3, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11. There are 8 values (even), so the median is the average of the two middle values: (5 + 7)/2 = 6.

book_ref.quote: The median is the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order

blocks.prompt: 14 Find the mode of 7, 3, 9, 3, 5, 11, 3 and 8. Can a data set have more than one mode?
blocks.explanation: 3 appears three times, more than any other value, so the mode is 3. Yes, there can be more than one mode if several numbers appear with the same highest frequency (e.g. 60 and 70 in 50, 60, 70, 70, 60, 90).

book_ref.quote: The mode helps us identify the most frequent or common value in the data

blocks.prompt: 15 Differentiate between mean and median.
blocks.explanation: Mean is the average value; median is the middle value of data arranged in order.

book_ref.quote: These measures give us a sense of the average or most common values in a dataset

rows: It is the average of all the numbers in a data set.
It is the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order.
Found by adding all numbers and dividing by the total number of values.
Odd count: the exact middle number; even count: the average of the two middle numbers.

blocks.prompt: 16 What are descriptive statistics? Why are they useful?
blocks.explanation: Descriptive statistics are used to summarize and organize data. Instead of looking at every individual piece of data, they give us a way to see the overall picture.

book_ref.quote: Instead of looking at every individual piece of data

blocks.prompt: 17 Ten students scored 50, 65, 75, 80, 85, 90, 95, 60, 70 and 88. Give the mean, the highest and the lowest score.
blocks.explanation: Sum = 758, so mean = 758/10 = 75.8. Highest score = 95; lowest score = 50. (The book prints 75.5; its correction gives 75.8.)

book_ref.quote: Imagine a group of 10 college students takes a math exam

blocks.prompt: 18 What are measures of dispersion? Name two of them.
blocks.explanation: Measures of dispersion tell us how spread out or scattered the data is, i.e. whether the data points are close to the mean or far from it. Two common measures are variance and standard deviation.

book_ref.quote: These help us understand whether the data points are close to the average (mean) or far from it

blocks.prompt: 19 What does a higher or a lower variance tell us about a data set?
blocks.explanation: Variance shows how much the numbers differ from the mean. A higher variance means the numbers are more spread out; a lower variance means they are closer to the mean.

book_ref.quote: A higher variance means that the numbers are more spread out

blocks.prompt: 20 Write the formula of variance and explain its symbols.
blocks.explanation: σ² = (1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)², with i from 1 to N, where xᵢ is each individual value, μ is the mean of the data set and N is the total number of values.

book_ref.quote: To calculate variance, we use the following mathematical formula

blocks.prompt: 21 Calculate the variance of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24.

book_ref.quote: Steps are involved in variance calculations

blocks.prompt: 22 Differentiate between variance and standard deviation.
blocks.explanation: Both measure spread; the standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

book_ref.quote: The standard deviation is similar to variance but provides a more practical number

rows: Shows how much the numbers in a data set differ from the mean.
Shows how spread out the numbers are in relation to the mean, as a more practical number.
σ² = (1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)²
σ = √((1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)²), the square root of the variance.

blocks.prompt: 23 The variance of a data set is 18. Find its standard deviation and say what a small value means.
blocks.explanation: Standard deviation = √18 ≈ 4.24. A small standard deviation means the values are closely packed around the mean; a large one means they are widely scattered.

book_ref.quote: This means that Class A's scores are closely packed around the mean

blocks.prompt: 24 Define probability and write its formula.
blocks.explanation:
Probability is the study of how likely an event is to happen; it helps us predict outcomes.
Probability = number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes.

book_ref.quote: It helps us predict outcomes based on what we know

blocks.prompt: 25 What is the probability of getting heads when a coin is flipped? Give reason.
blocks.explanation: There are two equally likely outcomes (heads or tails) and one of them is favourable, so P(heads) = 1/2 = 50%.

book_ref.quote: Consider flipping a coin. There are two possible outcomes: heads or tails

blocks.prompt: 26 Why are data collection and preparation crucial steps in any analysis?
blocks.explanation: Because the quality and relevance of the data directly impact the results and insights drawn from the study.

book_ref.quote: In order to carry out any research or analysis, data collection and preparation are crucial steps

blocks.prompt: 27 Define data collection and name its three methods.
blocks.explanation: Data collection is the process of gathering relevant information for a particular purpose. Its methods are surveys, observations and experiments.

book_ref.quote: These methods include surveys, observations, and experiments

blocks.prompt: 28 What is a survey? Name two means of conducting it.
blocks.explanation: A survey collects large amounts of data in a structured way by asking a predefined set of questions to a sample group. It can be conducted through online forms, telephone calls or face-to-face interviews.

book_ref.quote: Surveys are a commonly used method for collecting large amounts of data in a structured way

blocks.prompt: 29 How did the grocery store in Islamabad use its survey?
blocks.explanation: It gave a five-question survey to 50 customers over a weekend and analysed the responses to stock products that match customer demand, which improved business operations.

book_ref.quote: The collected responses are then analyzed to stock products that align with customer demand

blocks.prompt: 30 Give the chapter's example of data collection by observation.
blocks.explanation: A staff member of a restaurant watches which tables customers choose at lunchtime for one week. The restaurant then arranges its seating for comfort and smooth customer flow.

book_ref.quote: A restaurant is interested in knowing which tables are most frequently chosen by customers during lunchtime

blocks.prompt: 31 Differentiate between a survey and an observation.
blocks.explanation: A survey asks questions; an observation watches without interference.

book_ref.quote: Observation involves collecting data by watching or monitoring subjects

rows: Asks a predefined set of questions to a sample group.
Watches or monitors subjects in their natural environment.
Conducted through online forms, telephone calls or face-to-face interviews.
Gathers data on behaviours or phenomena without interference.
Example: five-question grocery store survey of 50 customers.
Example: watching restaurant table choices for one week.

blocks.prompt: 32 Differentiate between an observation and an experiment.
blocks.explanation: An observation does not interfere; an experiment changes variables on purpose.

book_ref.quote: Experiments involve manipulating one or more variables

rows: Collects data by watching subjects in their natural environment.
Manipulates one or more variables to find their effect on another variable.
No interference with the subjects.
Needs controlled environments for accurate measurement.
Used for behaviours, e.g. restaurant seating choices.
Used in scientific and engineering fields, e.g. printed notes test.

blocks.prompt: 33 Describe the teacher's printed-notes experiment briefly.
blocks.explanation: The teacher forms two groups: one receives printed notes, the other relies only on lectures. After one month both groups take the same test, and the results are compared to see whether printed notes improved performance.

book_ref.quote: After one month, both groups take the same test

blocks.prompt: 34 What does data preparation include?
blocks.explanation: Cleaning the data to remove errors or inconsistencies, organizing it in a meaningful way and converting it into a format suitable for analysis. Missing or incorrect data may need interpolation or statistical adjustments.

book_ref.quote: Once data has been collected, it is important to prepare it for analysis

blocks.prompt: 35 Why are data cleaning and transformation important?
blocks.explanation: Raw data often has errors, missing values or the wrong format. These issues must be fixed before analysis to ensure accurate results.

book_ref.quote: To ensure accurate results in analysis, it is important to fix these issues before moving forward

blocks.prompt: 36 Define data cleaning. Name the problems it fixes.
blocks.explanation: Data cleaning means correcting or removing any problems in the data: incorrect entries, missing values and duplicate data. If not fixed, the results will be misleading.

book_ref.quote: These problems can include incorrect entries, missing values, or duplicate data

blocks.prompt: 37 In Table 5.2, what two corrections are made in the cleaned data?
blocks.explanation:
1. The wrongly entered name "Alie" is corrected to "Ali".
2. Sara's missing grade is filled in (75), so the dataset is complete.

book_ref.quote: In this case, data cleaning would involve correcting any wrong names and finding the missing grades

blocks.prompt: 38 What is data transformation? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: After cleaning, data transformation changes the data into a format that is easy to work with, making it more suitable for analysis or modelling. Examples: converting data into different formats, creating new columns (or organizing data in a different way).

book_ref.quote: These changes help make the data more suitable for analysis or modeling

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between data cleaning and data transformation.
blocks.explanation: Cleaning fixes problems; transformation changes the format of clean data.

book_ref.quote: it is often necessary to transform it into a format that is easy to work with

rows: Corrects or removes problems in the data.
Changes clean data into a format that is easy to work with.
Fixes incorrect entries, missing values and duplicate data.
Converts formats, creates new columns or organizes data differently.
Done first, so that results are not misleading.
Done after cleaning, to suit analysis or modelling.

blocks.prompt: 40 Name three techniques for handling missing data.
blocks.explanation:
1. Imputation (estimating the missing value from existing data)
2. Flagging (noting that the value is not available)
3. Removal (excluding the record when missing entries are few)

book_ref.quote: There are different techniques to handle missing data

blocks.prompt: 41 Differentiate between imputation and flagging.
blocks.explanation: Imputation fills the gap with an estimate; flagging leaves the gap but marks it.

book_ref.quote: This approach allows the school to maintain a complete dataset while making a reasonable assumption

rows: Estimates the missing value using existing data.
Adds a note that the value is not available.
Example: Sara is given the class average grade of 82 for the time being.
Example: Sara's record is marked as missing a grade.
Keeps a complete dataset with a reasonable assumption.
Ensures transparency; the analysis goes on without filling the gap.

blocks.prompt: 42 When is removal of a record acceptable, and what is its risk?
blocks.explanation: Removal is acceptable when the number of missing entries is small and it does not significantly affect the overall understanding. Its risk is losing valuable information about that student.

book_ref.quote: This decision is acceptable if it does not significantly impact the overall understanding of student performance

blocks.prompt: 43 What is statistical modeling? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Statistical modeling uses data to make sense of the world and predict the future. Example: by analysing past grocery spending, a model estimates next month's grocery expenses, taking factors like family size or special occasions into account.

book_ref.quote: By analyzing that data, you can create a model to help you estimate your future grocery expenses

blocks.prompt: 44 List the five steps of building a statistical model.
blocks.explanation:
1. Define the problem
2. Collect data
3. Choose an algorithm
4. Train the model
5. Evaluate the model

book_ref.quote: Based on the problem and the data, we choose an algorithm

blocks.prompt: 45 What is an algorithm in model development? Name two popular ones.
blocks.explanation: Algorithms are methods that help us create a model; one is chosen based on the problem and the data. Two popular algorithms are linear regression and logistic regression.

book_ref.quote: Some popular algorithms are linear regression and logistic regression

blocks.prompt: 46 Why is the model evaluated with new data?
blocks.explanation: Testing with new data shows how well the model works on data it has not learned from. This step ensures the model makes good predictions.

book_ref.quote: This step is very important to ensure the model makes good predictions

blocks.prompt: 47 What is linear regression? Write its formula.
blocks.explanation:
Linear regression is a common statistical model used to understand the relationship between two variables and to predict one from the other.
Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε

book_ref.quote: It is often used to predict one variable based on another

blocks.prompt: 48 Differentiate between the independent and the dependent variable in linear regression.
blocks.explanation: The independent variable is the cause; the dependent variable is the effect.

book_ref.quote: Here, the number of customers is our independent variable (X), and the daily earnings are the dependent variable (Y)

rows: The cause; it is used to make the prediction.
The effect; it is the value being predicted.
Written as X in Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε.
Written as Y in Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε.
Fruit stall: number of customers.
Fruit stall: daily earnings in rupees.

blocks.prompt: 49 Differentiate between slope and intercept in a linear regression model.
blocks.explanation: The slope is the change in Y per unit of X; the intercept is Y when X = 0.

book_ref.quote: is the slope, which shows how much Y changes with each unit increase in X

rows: Shows how much Y changes with each unit increase in X.
The starting value of Y when X = 0.
Fruit stall: each new customer adds 40 rupees.
Fruit stall: 100 rupees earned even with no customers.
Found from the data: 200/5 = 40.
Found from one data point: 500 − 40 × 10 = 100.

blocks.prompt: 50 Using Earnings = 100 + 40 × Customers, predict the earnings for 18 customers.

book_ref.quote: This means that with 22 customers, you can expect to earn around 980 rupees

blocks.prompt: 51 A model predicts 1,220 rupees for 28 customers but 1,250 rupees were earned. What is the error, and what does it show?
blocks.explanation: Error = predicted − actual = 1,220 − 1,250 = −30 rupees. The prediction was close but not perfect, showing that real-world data often has some variation.

book_ref.quote: While the prediction was close, it's not perfect, showing that real-world data often has some variation

blocks.prompt: 52 Give two suggestions for improving a statistical model.
blocks.explanation:
1. Use more data points for better accuracy.
2. Regularly update the model with new data to keep it relevant.
(Also: include relevant factors such as family size; test predictions against actual values.)

book_ref.quote: Include relevant factors like family size or special events that may affect spending

blocks.prompt: 53 Differentiate between linear regression and logistic regression.
blocks.explanation: Linear regression predicts exact numbers; logistic regression predicts a probability for a yes/no outcome.

book_ref.quote: Logistic regression is different from linear regression because it doesn

rows: Predicts an exact number of the dependent variable.
Predicts the probability of a yes or no outcome.
Output can be any value, e.g. 980 rupees.
Output is a probability between 0 and 1, e.g. 0.85.
Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε
Example: daily earnings from number of customers.
Example: pass or fail from hours studied.

blocks.prompt: 54 A logistic regression model gives 0.85 for passing an exam. Interpret this value.
blocks.explanation: The value is a probability: there is an 85% chance that the student will pass, based on the study hours.

book_ref.quote: This means it tells us how likely something is to happen

blocks.prompt: 55 In the logistic model of study hours, what do β₀ and β₁ represent?
blocks.explanation:
β₀ is the intercept: the log-odds of passing when no hours are studied.
β₁ is the coefficient of hours studied: how much the log-odds of passing change with each additional hour.

book_ref.quote: is the intercept of the model, which represents the log-odds of passing when no hours are studied

blocks.prompt: 56 With P(pass) = 1 / (1 + e^−(1 + 0.6 × Hours)), find the probability of passing for 0 hours of study.

book_ref.quote: This means that for each hour studied, the likelihood of passing the exam increases

blocks.prompt: 57 What is clustering? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Clustering is a way of grouping similar things together based on their characteristics. Example: dividing the students of a class into groups of students who perform similarly in maths and English.

book_ref.quote: Clustering helps us do that by creating groups of students who perform similarly

blocks.prompt: 58 How does K-means decide which student joins which cluster?
blocks.explanation: It calculates the distance (Euclidean distance) of each student's scores from every cluster centre and assigns the student to the nearest centre.

book_ref.quote: K-means clustering is one of the simplest and most popular techniques to group data

blocks.prompt: 59 Find the Euclidean distance between the score points (85, 70) and (60, 60).

book_ref.quote: We calculate the distance of each student

blocks.prompt: 60 When does the K-means algorithm stop?
blocks.explanation: Steps 3 (assign to nearest centre) and 4 (recalculate centres) are repeated until the centres no longer change; then the clusters are stable.

book_ref.quote: This process continues until the centers no longer change

blocks.prompt: 61 A cluster has students with scores (85, 70), (90, 65) and (60, 60). Find its new centre.

book_ref.quote: by finding the average position (average scores) of the students in each cluster

blocks.prompt: 62 What is model evaluation?
blocks.explanation: Once a model is built, checking how well it performs and understanding the results it provides is called model evaluation.

book_ref.quote: This is called model evaluation

blocks.prompt: 63 Differentiate between error metrics and accuracy metrics.
blocks.explanation: Error metrics measure how far predictions are off; accuracy metrics count how many were right.

book_ref.quote: Performance metrics help us measure how well a model is doing

rows: Measure how much the predictions differ from the actual values.
Tell how many of the predictions were correct.
Example: predicted grocery bill 8,000 rupees, actual 10,000; the difference is the error.
Example: how often a pass/fail model was right.

blocks.prompt: 64 What does interpreting a model's output mean? Give an example of a conclusion.
blocks.explanation: It means understanding what the results tell us. Example: if a linear regression model shows that hours studied strongly affect exam scores, we conclude that students should study more hours to improve their scores.

book_ref.quote: we can conclude that students should study more hours to improve their scores

blocks.prompt: 65 Name two ethical considerations in building models, with one example each.
blocks.explanation:
1. Fairness and bias: a loan model should not unfairly favour one group of people over another.
2. Data privacy: customer data used for models should be secure and not shared without permission.

book_ref.quote: When building models, it is important to consider the ethical implications, such as fairness and privacy

blocks.prompt: 66 Define data visualization.
blocks.explanation: Data visualization is the process of representing data in a visual format, such as graphs or charts. It helps us quickly grasp patterns, trends and insights from data.

book_ref.quote: Data visualization is the process of representing data in a visual format

blocks.prompt: 67 Which visualization would you use to (i) compare sales of products and (ii) see the spread of exam scores of three classes?
blocks.explanation:
To compare sales of different products: a bar chart (it compares categories).
To compare the score spread of three classes: a boxplot (it shows median, quartiles and outliers).

book_ref.quote: Data visualization is a powerful way to understand complex information

blocks.prompt: 68 Differentiate between a bar chart and a histogram.
blocks.explanation: A bar chart compares categories; a histogram shows how a dataset is distributed.

book_ref.quote: Each bar represents a category

rows: Used for comparing different categories.
Used to show the distribution of a dataset.
Each bar is a category; its height (or length) is the value.
Data is grouped into bins or intervals showing how often values occur.
Example: sales of different products in a store.
Example: distribution of scores in a maths exam.

blocks.prompt: 69 Differentiate between a line graph and a scatterplot.
blocks.explanation: A line graph shows a trend over time; a scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables.

book_ref.quote: If you track the temperature over a week, a line graph will show how the temperature rises and falls each day

rows: Shows trends over time.
Displays the relationship between two variables.
Data points are connected with a line.
Each point is a separate observation; its position gives both values.
Example: temperature over a week.
Example: hours studied and exam scores.

blocks.prompt: 70 What is a boxplot? What does it display?
blocks.explanation: A boxplot (whisker plot) summarizes a data distribution by displaying the median, quartiles and potential outliers. It gives a visual summary of data variability, e.g. comparing exam scores of different classes.

book_ref.quote: They provide a visual summary of data variability

blocks.prompt: 71 How does visualization help us make sense of large amounts of information?
blocks.explanation: It turns numbers into easy-to-understand charts and graphs, so large amounts of information can be understood quickly.

book_ref.quote: visualization data helps us make sense of large amounts of information by turning numbers into easy-to-understand charts and graphs

blocks.prompt: 72 Write the four steps for creating a chart in Excel or Google Sheets.
blocks.explanation:
1. Enter your data into the spreadsheet.
2. Select (highlight) the data.
3. Choose a chart type from the Insert tab.
4. Customize the chart, e.g. add axis labels.

book_ref.quote: Start by entering your data into the spreadsheet

blocks.prompt: 73 Why should labels be added to a chart?
blocks.explanation: Labels, such as months on the x-axis and sales figures on the y-axis, make the chart clearer and easier to interpret.

book_ref.quote: This makes the chart easier to interpret
